# Dr Aino Kaarnevuo

**Principal Lecturer in Music Pedagogy and Director of Teaching Development**  
Kaarensalmi University of Applied Sciences, Tampere, Finland  
CV updated: 21 September 2026

## Education and appointments

I completed a master's degree in music education in 2002 and a doctorate in education in 2010. My doctoral research examined how instrumental teachers communicated assessment criteria during individual lessons, using recorded teaching, stimulated recall and analysis of student work.

I joined Kaarensalmi University of Applied Sciences as a lecturer in 2003, became senior lecturer in 2011 and principal lecturer in 2018. Since 2021 I have also directed teaching development. My responsibilities include staff development, review of practical assessment and coordination of curriculum changes with programme boards. I remain involved in teaching undergraduate instrumental pedagogy and supervising practice-based dissertations.

## Research and teaching responsibilities

My work concerns the relationship between instructions, access arrangements and what students can demonstrate in practical assessments. I use classroom observation, interviews and repeated assessment alongside descriptive and inferential analysis. I have experience integrating these forms of evidence within institutional teaching reviews.

I coordinated the internally funded project Studio Instructions and Shared Access during 2025. I was responsible for the common assessment protocol, reporting to the institutional teaching boards and reconciliation of the project accounts.

In the consortium's signed teaching collaboration, I chair the academic coordination group. Each institution retains responsibility for its own awards, student records, employment arrangements, contracts, finances and curriculum approvals.

## Methodological experience

My practical experience includes rubric development, assessor moderation, paired assessment analysis and reflexive thematic analysis. For the studio pilot, I worked with local teachers to distinguish musical execution from the explanation and adaptation of teaching instructions. I have also used audio annotation to examine pauses and overlapping speech in recorded lessons.

I teach in Finnish and English. My teaching-development work includes consultations with students about access arrangements and revision of practical assessment instructions.

The institutions signed their teaching collaboration agreement on 17 June 2024. ## Named responsibilities

Dr Aino Kaarnevuo coordinates the collaboration from Finland. Petra Vraneković, senior lecturer in instrumental pedagogy at Velinac, leads practical teaching moderation and maintains the Croatian staff-development record. Lotte Verhaegelin, head of practical learning at Ravelbeek, coordinates the recording of curriculum decisions and follow-up with programme boards.

Maija Kuusentola is Kaarensalmi's language-support lecturer. She holds a master's degree in applied linguistics awarded in 2009 and completed 60 ECTS of teacher pedagogical studies in 2011. Her current teaching includes academic language support and accessible instructional writing. She coordinates multilingual adaptation with local language teachers and organises student review of the materials. Her duties include plain-language revision, terminology alignment and checking comprehension across language versions.

Eeva Rantakoski is the consortium accessibility officer, employed by Kaarensalmi. Her remit covers evaluation accessibility, consent formats, assessment instructions and procedures for requesting adjustments. She reports access problems to the coordination group and maintains a confidential route for students who prefer not to disclose an access need to their assessor. Local programme heads retain responsibility for implementing adjustments.

The collaboration has three existing teaching studios, one at each institution. Each has audio recording equipment, an induction loop and a display for written instructions. Adjustable seating, accessible electronic handouts and captioned teaching clips were used in the completed pilot. The studios remain in ordinary teaching use. Technical support is provided by studio technicians and covers studio recording and caption correction.

All partners have institutionally licensed captioning software available through their teaching systems. Automatic captions require human correction, particularly for musical terminology, overlapping speech and Croatian inflections. Student recordings remain within institutionally controlled storage.

## Placement register and baseline records

At its meeting on 25 September 2026, the coordination group agreed to explore a network of 12 external teaching placements. At the close of this record, no placement agreements have been signed and no placement sites, mentors or students have been recruited for the network.

Historical placement registers were kept separately by each institution. They record hosts, dates and supervisors, but do not identify which placements met a common accessibility definition. The number of existing accessible placements cannot be established from these records.

The student-record systems lack a harmonised disability classification and a compatible participation numerator and denominator. A baseline rate of disabled-student participation cannot be calculated from them. Language-support and caption requests are recorded as service requests.

# Final report: Studio Instructions and Shared Access

Project period: 1 January–31 December 2025  
Final report issued: 18 February 2026  
Institutional uptake addendum: 30 September 2026  
Coordinator: Dr Aino Kaarnevuo

## Purpose and financial record

The project examined whether more explicit, accessible instructions could support collaborative practical teaching in undergraduate music pedagogy. It addressed uncertainty about how students understood a teaching task, requested clarification and demonstrated an adaptation for another learner. Musical performance quality was considered separately from these pedagogical outcomes.

The project received EUR 48,000 through a joint internal teaching-development award, with EUR 16,000 contributed by each institution. There was no external research grant. Final expenditure equalled the award: EUR 30,000 for staff release, EUR 9,000 for technical support, EUR 6,000 for access support and EUR 3,000 for travel. The account was closed in February 2026.

## Participants and teaching intervention

The pilot enrolled 72 students, comprising 24 at each institution. Recruitment took place within existing undergraduate music-pedagogy modules. Participation in research was voluntary and did not determine course grades. Students could receive the revised teaching materials without consenting to research use of their work.

Teachers used a common sequence: written and spoken instructions, a demonstration with corrected captions, a comprehension check and a collaborative microteaching task. Students could consult terminology sheets in Finnish, Croatian, Dutch and English. Local teachers checked terminology and students commented on comprehensibility.

The intervention ran within one teaching semester. All participating classes received it; there was no untreated comparison group and no random allocation.

## Assessment and quantitative findings

The baseline and follow-up tasks required students to explain a rehearsal instruction, identify an access obstacle and adapt the instruction while preserving its musical purpose. A common rubric assessed instructional clarity, responsiveness and justification. Musical execution was recorded separately and was not included in the pedagogical learning score. Local assessors moderated sample work together before scoring; the same local teams assessed both occasions and were aware of timing.

Paired assessments were available for 60 students, with 20 at each institution. This represents 83.3% of enrolment. The remaining 12 students completed the baseline task but had no usable follow-up assessment; four were missing at each institution.

The complete-case mean improvement was 0.18 SD, with a 95% CI of -0.03 to 0.39. Change scores were expressed using the pooled baseline standard deviation of the paired sample. The interval was calculated from the paired changes, treating that standardising quantity as fixed. It is an individual-level descriptive interval and does not account for shared class or institutional influences.

## Interviews and interpretation

Interviews included 18 students, six per institution, and nine teachers, three per institution. These were purposive samples drawn from the participating classes. Student selection sought contrasting accounts of participation and comprehension.

Two analysts read the interview transcripts, developed interpretive memos and discussed differences in coding. Students described written instructions as useful when spoken directions were rapid. Some described captions as distracting during simultaneous playing and listening. Teachers reported that terminology checks made assumptions about prior knowledge more visible.

The project generated annotated teaching materials, rubric examples and a staff seminar pack. Audio annotation identified pauses and overlapping instructions for teacher discussion.

## Ethics and institutional uptake

Research review was completed before recruitment under institutional approval KAA-EDU-2024-11. Partners adopted the consent and local data-handling procedures before collecting records. Participation could be withdrawn without a grading penalty. Identifiable teaching recordings were restricted to authorised staff; public materials contain recreated examples rather than student recordings.

The approval covers the 2025 pilot only. As of 30 September 2026, the collaboration's research approval register contains no subsequent evaluation approval.

By 30 September 2026, programme boards at all three institutions had approved the revised instruction sequence within the participating music-pedagogy modules. Staff seminars had been delivered at each institution, and the common material pack was available through institutional teaching repositories.

## Limitations

The confidence interval includes both a small decline and an improvement. Routine teaching, familiarity with the task and assessor expectations could explain the observed change; the study does not establish an intervention effect.

No missing-outcome imputation was undertaken. Missingness was not classified by disability or access need, preventing assessment of whether follow-up loss was socially patterned. The report did not estimate separate language effects, disability subgroup effects or institution-specific effects; the design and available records did not support those comparisons.

The uptake record documents board decisions and delivery of staff development. It contains no post-adoption assessment of sustained learner outcomes. Curriculum uptake is confined to the participating modules. External reuse had not been measured. The terminology sheets have not undergone programme-board review or validation as a translation curriculum.

# Dr Aino Kaarnevuo

**Principal Lecturer in Music Pedagogy and Director of Teaching Development**  
Kaarensalmi University of Applied Arts, Tampere, Finland  
CV updated: 21 September 2026

## Education and appointments

I completed a master's degree in music education in 2002 and a doctorate in education in 2010. My doctoral research examined how instrumental teachers communicated assessment criteria during individual lessons, using recorded teaching, stimulated recall and analysis of student work.

I joined Kaarensalmi University of Applied Arts as a lecturer in 2003, became senior lecturer in 2011 and principal lecturer in 2018. Since 2021 I have also directed teaching development. My responsibilities include staff development, review of practical assessment and coordination of curriculum changes with programme boards. I remain involved in teaching undergraduate instrumental pedagogy and supervising practice-based dissertations.

## Research and teaching responsibilities

My work concerns the relationship between instructions, access arrangements and what students can demonstrate in practical assessments. I use classroom observation, interviews and repeated assessment alongside descriptive and inferential analysis. I have experience integrating these forms of evidence within institutional teaching reviews. I do not treat concert attendance, public performance or student satisfaction as substitutes for assessed learning.

I coordinated the internally funded project Studio Instructions and Shared Access during 2025. This was my first completed teaching study involving all the present consortium institutions. I was responsible for the common assessment protocol, reporting to the institutional teaching boards and reconciliation of the project accounts. The project investigated existing courses rather than establishing a new qualification.

In the consortium's signed teaching collaboration, I chair the academic coordination group. Each institution retains responsibility for its own awards, student records, employment arrangements and curriculum approvals. My coordination role does not give me authority to approve another institution's modules or to sign agreements on its behalf.

## Methodological experience

My practical experience includes rubric development, assessor moderation, paired assessment analysis and reflexive thematic analysis. For the studio pilot, I worked with local teachers to distinguish musical execution from the explanation and adaptation of teaching instructions. I have also used audio annotation to examine pauses and overlapping speech in recorded lessons. I have not led a language-model benchmarking programme, trained an acoustic foundation model or managed a multilingual model leaderboard.

I teach in Finnish and English. My role in multilingual work is pedagogical coordination; specialist language adaptation is led by the consortium's qualified language-support lecturer. I have experience consulting students about access arrangements but do not claim clinical expertise in sensory impairment. The consortium accessibility officer oversees evaluation accessibility and the handling of access-related disclosures.

# Final report: Studio Instructions and Shared Access

Project period: 1 January–31 December 2025  
Final report issued: 18 February 2026  
Institutional uptake addendum: 30 September 2026  
Coordinator: Dr Aino Kaarnevuo

## Purpose and financial record

The project examined whether more explicit, accessible instructions could support collaborative practical teaching in undergraduate music pedagogy. It addressed uncertainty about how students understood a teaching task, requested clarification and demonstrated an adaptation for another learner. Musical performance quality was considered separately from these pedagogical outcomes.

The project received EUR 48,000 through a joint internal teaching-development award, with EUR 16,000 contributed by each institution. There was no external research grant. Final expenditure equalled the award: EUR 30,000 for staff release, EUR 9,000 for technical support, EUR 6,000 for access support and EUR 3,000 for travel. The account was closed in February 2026.

## Participants and teaching intervention

The pilot enrolled 72 students, comprising 24 at each institution. Recruitment took place within existing undergraduate music-pedagogy modules. Participation in research was voluntary and did not determine course grades. Students could receive the revised teaching materials without consenting to research use of their work.

Teachers used a common sequence: written and spoken instructions, a demonstration with corrected captions, a comprehension check and a collaborative microteaching task. Students could consult terminology sheets in Finnish, Croatian, Dutch and English. Local teachers checked terminology and students commented on comprehensibility. These checks did not establish psychometric equivalence between language versions or validate a translation curriculum.

The intervention ran within one teaching semester. All participating classes received it; there was no untreated comparison group and no random allocation. Routine teaching, familiarity with the task and assessor expectations are therefore alternative explanations for any change.

## Assessment and quantitative findings

The baseline and follow-up tasks required students to explain a rehearsal instruction, identify an access obstacle and adapt the instruction while preserving its musical purpose. A common rubric assessed instructional clarity, responsiveness and justification. Musical execution was recorded separately and was not included in the pedagogical learning score. Local assessors moderated sample work together before scoring; the same local teams assessed both occasions and were aware of timing.

Paired assessments were available for 60 students, with 20 at each institution. This represents 83.3% of enrolment. The remaining 12 students completed the baseline task but had no usable follow-up assessment; four were missing at each institution. Missingness was not classified by disability or access need, and the study cannot establish whether assessment loss was socially patterned.

The complete-case mean improvement was 0.18 SD, with a 95% CI of -0.03 to 0.39. Change scores were expressed using the pooled baseline standard deviation of the paired sample. The interval was calculated from the paired changes, treating that standardising quantity as fixed. It is an individual-level descriptive interval and does not account for shared class or institutional influences.

The estimate is compatible with a small decline as well as an improvement. It does not demonstrate an intervention effect. No missing-outcome imputation was undertaken. The report did not estimate separate language effects, disability subgroup effects or institution-specific effects; the design and available records did not support those comparisons.

## Interviews and interpretation

Interviews included 18 students, six per institution, and nine teachers, three per institution. These were purposive samples drawn from the participating classes, not independent additional cohorts. Student selection sought contrasting accounts of participation and comprehension; it did not use a disability sampling frame.

Two analysts read the interview transcripts, developed interpretive memos and discussed differences in coding. Students described written instructions as useful when spoken directions were rapid. Some described captions as distracting during simultaneous playing and listening. Teachers reported that terminology checks made assumptions about prior knowledge more visible. These themes explain reported experiences; their frequency was not used to estimate population prevalence or learning gains.

The project generated annotated teaching materials, rubric examples and a staff seminar pack. Audio annotation identified pauses and overlapping instructions for teacher discussion. No language-model training or leaderboard evaluation formed part of the study. Public performances associated with the modules were not analysed as evidence of improved learning.

## Ethics, uptake and remaining limitations

Research review was completed before recruitment under institutional approval KAA-EDU-2024-11. Partners adopted the consent and local data-handling procedures before collecting records. Participation could be withdrawn without a grading penalty. Identifiable teaching recordings were restricted to authorised staff; public materials contain recreated examples rather than student recordings.

By 30 September 2026, programme boards at all three institutions had approved the revised instruction sequence within existing music-pedagogy modules. This is adoption within named modules, not approval of a new qualification or institution-wide validation. Staff seminars had been delivered at each institution, and the common material pack was available through institutional teaching repositories. External reuse had not been measured.

The uptake record documents board decisions and delivery of staff development. It contains no post-adoption assessment of sustained learner outcomes. The pilot also provides no baseline rate of disabled-student participation and no inventory of accessible external placements. Its findings concern a studio teaching intervention in a self-selected research sample.

# Selected publications and associated materials

Bibliography verified: 23 September 2026

The 4 publications below are published journal articles. None is under review or awaiting acceptance. The list distinguishes conceptual and teaching-method contributions from the empirical pilot report. Repository teaching materials are separate outputs and are not counted as additional publications.

1. **Kaarnevuo, A., and Vraneković, P. (2023). Making rehearsal instructions assessable: A rubric for pedagogical explanation.** *Journal of Situated Studio Learning*. DOI: 10.99999/pb.v2-accessible-music-teaching-alliance.2023.1

   This methodological article explains the distinction between successful musical execution and a student's ability to justify an instructional choice. It presents rubric construction and worked assessment examples. It does not report an intervention effect or validate comparisons between different language versions. Its categories informed the later common studio assessment.

2. **Kuusentola, M., Kaarnevuo, A., and Verhaegelin, L. (2024). Terminology negotiation in multilingual music-pedagogy seminars.** *Review of Multilingual Arts Instruction*. DOI: 10.99999/pb.v2-accessible-music-teaching-alliance.2024.2

   This teaching-method paper examines how staff can make ambiguous rehearsal terminology explicit. It presents parallel instructional examples and a procedure for student comprehension checks. The article concerns language support within arts education; it neither validates a translation curriculum nor establishes equivalence between language tests.

3. **Rantakoski, E., Vraneković, P., and Kaarnevuo, A. (2025). Caption choice and learner control in collaborative rehearsal teaching.** *Studies in Rehearsal Pedagogy and Access*. DOI: 10.99999/pb.v2-accessible-music-teaching-alliance.2025.3

   This practice paper describes caption review, access consultations and the option to separate viewing from playing. Its examples illustrate adjustments and their practical tradeoffs. It does not quantify disabled-student participation or classify historical placement venues as accessible.

4. **Kaarnevuo, A., Vraneković, P., Verhaegelin, L., Kuusentola, M., and Rantakoski, E. (2026). Accessible instructions in music-pedagogy studios: A three-institution paired pilot.** *Higher Arts Curriculum Inquiry*. DOI: 10.99999/pb.v2-accessible-music-teaching-alliance.2026.4

   Published in July 2026, this article reports the completed studio pilot described in the final report. It presents the complete-case assessment estimate alongside interview interpretation and discusses the absence of a control group. It is the same study and sample, not an independent replication.

## Access to supporting material

Accepted manuscripts and the recreated teaching examples are held in the partners' institutional repositories. The seminar pack includes accessible text versions and corrected captions. Raw student recordings and identifiable interview transcripts are not publicly released. The teaching materials have been used in consortium staff seminars; repository availability alone has not been counted as evidence of external curriculum adoption.

# Final report: Studio Instructions and Shared Access

Project period: 1 January–31 December 2025  
Final report issued: 18 February 2026  
Institutional uptake addendum: 30 September 2026  
Coordinator: Dr Aino Kaarnevuo

## Purpose and financial record

The project examined whether more explicit, accessible instructions could support collaborative practical teaching in undergraduate music pedagogy. It addressed uncertainty about how students understood a teaching task, requested clarification and demonstrated an adaptation for another learner. Musical performance quality was considered separately from these pedagogical outcomes.

The project received EUR 48,000 through a joint internal teaching-development award, with EUR 16,000 contributed by each institution. There was no external research grant. Final expenditure equalled the award: EUR 30,000 for staff release, EUR 9,000 for technical support, EUR 6,000 for access support and EUR 3,000 for travel. The account was closed in February 2026.

## Participants and teaching intervention

The pilot enrolled 72 students, comprising 24 at each institution. Recruitment took place within existing undergraduate music-pedagogy modules. Participation in research was voluntary and did not determine course grades. Students could receive the revised teaching materials without consenting to research use of their work.

Teachers used a common sequence: written and spoken instructions, a demonstration with corrected captions, a comprehension check and a collaborative microteaching task. Students could consult terminology sheets in Finnish, Croatian, Dutch and English. Local teachers checked terminology and students commented on comprehensibility. The language materials were teaching resources reviewed through local terminology and comprehension checks.

The intervention ran within one teaching semester. All participating classes received it; there was no untreated comparison group and no random allocation. Routine teaching, familiarity with the task and assessor expectations are therefore alternative explanations for any change.

## Assessment and quantitative findings

The baseline and follow-up tasks required students to explain a rehearsal instruction, identify an access obstacle and adapt the instruction while preserving its musical purpose. A common rubric assessed instructional clarity, responsiveness and justification. Musical execution was recorded separately and was not included in the pedagogical learning score. Local assessors moderated sample work together before scoring; the same local teams assessed both occasions and were aware of timing.

Paired assessments were available for 60 students, with 20 at each institution. This represents 83.3% of enrolment. The remaining 12 students completed the baseline task but had no usable follow-up assessment; four were missing at each institution. Missingness was not classified by disability or access need, and the study cannot establish whether assessment loss was socially patterned.

The complete-case mean improvement was 0.18 SD, with a 95% CI of -0.03 to 0.39. Change scores were expressed using the pooled baseline standard deviation of the paired sample. The interval was calculated from the paired changes, treating that standardising quantity as fixed. It is an individual-level descriptive interval and does not account for shared class or institutional influences.

The estimate is compatible with a small decline as well as an improvement. It does not demonstrate an intervention effect. No missing-outcome imputation was undertaken. The report did not estimate separate language effects, disability subgroup effects or institution-specific effects; the design and available records did not support those comparisons.

## Interviews and interpretation

Interviews included 18 students, six per institution, and nine teachers, three per institution. These were purposive samples drawn from the participating classes. Student selection sought contrasting accounts of participation and comprehension.

Two analysts read the interview transcripts, developed interpretive memos and discussed differences in coding. Students described written instructions as useful when spoken directions were rapid. Some described captions as distracting during simultaneous playing and listening. Teachers reported that terminology checks made assumptions about prior knowledge more visible. These themes explain reported experiences; their frequency was not used to estimate population prevalence or learning gains.

The project generated annotated teaching materials, rubric examples and a staff seminar pack. Audio annotation identified pauses and overlapping instructions for teacher discussion.

## Ethics, uptake and remaining limitations

Research review was completed before recruitment under institutional approval KAA-EDU-2024-11. Partners adopted the consent and local data-handling procedures before collecting records. Participation could be withdrawn without a grading penalty. Identifiable teaching recordings were restricted to authorised staff; public materials contain recreated examples rather than student recordings.

By 30 September 2026, programme boards at all three institutions had approved the revised instruction sequence within the participating music-pedagogy modules. Staff seminars had been delivered at each institution, and the common material pack was available through institutional teaching repositories. External reuse had not been measured.

The uptake record documents board decisions and delivery of staff development. It contains no post-adoption assessment of sustained learner outcomes. Curriculum uptake is confined to the participating modules. Review of the multilingual resources has covered terminology and comprehensibility; curriculum validation remains unestablished. The pilot findings concern a studio teaching intervention in a self-selected research sample.
